topic: The Streaming Ad Bust: Linear’s Comeback
description: How streaming platforms’ ad-load experiments collided with subscriber churn, while FAST and ad-supported incumbents gained share—turning 2023’s “everything goes viral” into 2024–2025’s ad-budget reshuffle.

🚨 STREAMING’S BIGGEST PIVOT: Ads didn’t “save” the business—FAST did.

In this chart-race visualization, we track the money shift from subscription-first streaming toward ad-supported streaming (FAST) and ad-heavy video (YouTube), while traditional TV ad spend keeps bleeding.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The $100B Ad Shift: Streaming’s “fix” didn’t work—FAST won.

Remember when streaming ads were supposed to be the golden lever? From 2018 to 2020, ad budgets still chased video, and everyone believed the future was subscription-first—then monetization would “click.” But the timeline tells a different story: the moment platforms started turning up ad loads to chase revenue, viewers didn’t just tolerate it… they bounced. Meanwhile, the ad ecosystem didn’t disappear—it rerouted.

By 2021, YouTube’s ad engine was clearly in control, climbing from about $27.4B (2021) to roughly $31.5B in 2022 and ~$34.0B in 2023—because it’s built for intent and frequency. That’s why the ad dollars kept showing up there, even as streaming’s measurement debates dragged on.

Then 2023 hits—and this is the gut-punch. Linear incumbents (US TV & radio total) fell from $74.4B (2022) to ~$66.8B (2023), while FAST accelerated from $18.9B (2022) to ~$22.4B (2023). FAST wasn’t trying to “recreate the subscription relationship.” It was leaning into the ad reality: cheaper inventory, clearer targeting, and faster scaling.

By 2024–2025, the chart race gets ruthless. FAST rises to ~$26.9B (2024) and ~$29.5B (2025). Hulu Ads follows the disciplined path too—about $4.8B (2022) → $5.5B (2023) → ~$6.7B (2024) → ~$7.4B (2025). Meanwhile, Netflix’s ad revenue is basically near-zero on this timeline until its ad-tier rollout becomes measurable: ~ $5B (2024) and ~$7B (2025).

Question: If you were an advertiser with a fixed budget in 2025, would you chase YouTube’s reach, or ride the FAST growth curve?

Follow/subscribe for more chart-race market timelines—this series is built for instant “who won?” moments.
facebook_caption:
Streaming advertising was expected to rescue subscription-first models—but the money rerouted to platforms built for ad monetization. This timeline comparison contrasts ad revenue growth at YouTube and FAST channels against the decline in traditional US linear TV & radio advertising spend.

From 2018 to 2022, linear advertising remained large (about $70.5B to $74.4B), while ad-heavy video grew steadily. In 2023, linear spend dropped to approximately $66.8B as streaming platforms faced churn and ad-load friction. At the same time, FAST accelerated from about $18.9B (2022) to roughly $22.4B (2023). By 2024–2025, FAST continues scaling (~$26.9B to ~$29.5B), while Hulu ad revenue trends upward (~$6.7B in 2024 to ~$7.4B in 2025). Netflix’s ad revenue on this specific series becomes measurable later (~$5B in 2024; ~$7B in 2025), highlighting how quickly incumbents and ad-native ecosystems captured the budget.

Which channel do you think will absorb the next wave of ad dollars: YouTube or FAST?
threads_caption:
Hot take: streaming didn’t “solve” ads—FAST did. 📺💥

From 2022 → 2025, FAST goes from ~$18.9B to ~$29.5B, while linear US TV & radio keeps sliding (about $74.4B → $60B). YouTube keeps stacking ad revenue too—basically the reliable place advertisers kept trusting.

If you had to pick ONE to bet on for ad growth right now: YouTube or FAST?
